text: King Louis XIII had an obsession with watching women give birth. Back in those days, it was normal for women to typically give birth in upright positions, so with gravity assisting. But King Louis XIII needed the best possible view he could get. And so he would make the women lay on their backs with their legs up and he would put a chair at the end of the bed so that he could watch vehemently. Does this sound familiar? Obies adopted that from Louis XIII. It's actually completely counterintuitive to a normal physiologic efficient labor in birth. This makes it so that the pelvis can't open efficiently and baby can't get into a favorable position, so it actually hinders the process. So there's a popular claim going around, which the woman in this video mentions, that today women commonly give birth lying on their backs because King Louis XIV had a king for watching women give birth. And apparently, this position gave him a better view. By the way, she says Louis XIII, but the story is actually about Louis XIV. So is there any truth to this? Well, the problem is that there's no solid historical evidence supporting this story. For example, a 1987 paper published in the American Journal of Public Health discusses this theory. Even there, the author only says that some scholars have made this claim without providing convincing historical evidence that the king actually demanded such a change. And here is something interesting. Back in 1598, a French surgeon named Jacques Guillemot was already recommending giving birth reclining in bed. That is 40 years before Louis XIV was even born. So no, we have no good reason to believe that some French kings' sexual preferences are responsible for how women give birth today. But then why did lying down childbirth become so common? Well, historically, women gave birth in many different positions. Squatting, kneeling, sitting on birthing stools, and yes, sometimes lying down. In 1668, another French physician, Francois Morisot, published an influential medical book recommending that women give birth in bed, with their upper bodies slightly raised. And his reasoning included women's comfort, easier breathing, and avoiding the need to move them into bed after delivery. And as childbirth increasingly moved into hospitals, lying down positions became more widespread, partly because they were also convenient for medical professionals. But what about today? Why do women still frequently give birth lying down or semi-reclined? Well, there are several reasons. First, epidurals. A type of anesthesia commonly used during childbirth to reduce pain. But they can also make standing, squatting, or moving around more difficult. Second, labor can last many hours. Lying down allows women to rest and conserve energy. And some women simply prefer supportive positions. Third, medical monitoring and interventions. Certain positions make it easier for doctors and midwives to examine the patient and assist with complicated deliveries. Now, does that mean lying down is always the best position for giving birth? Not necessarily. Research suggests upright positions have certain advantages, especially for women without epidurals. But here's something interesting. A large British randomized trial involving over 3,000 first-time mothers with epidurals actually found that women assigned to lying down positions had a higher chance of giving birth without forceps, vacuum assistance, or a C-section than women assigned to upright positions. And importantly, these were primarily side-lying positions, not flat on the back. So the position matters and different circumstances call for different approaches. Modern medical guidelines generally encourage women to choose whatever position they find comfortable and medically appropriate. And that, I think, is the important distinction. So yes, giving birth lying down can have disadvantages, but there are also a number of legitimate reasons why it became and remains so common. And there's certainly no convincing evidence that we are doing this today because some French king wanted a better view.
